power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

# display table -----------------------------------

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p=0.17", "p =0.088", "p=0.67", "p=0.68" ), Sentence = c("Then, we did the regression analysis for male and female subgroup, and we found that for male group, the age was significantly negatively associated with reporting discrepancy (β =-2.30, SE=0.73, (t(88)=-3.13, p=0.002) while female group doesn't (β =-0.75, SE=0.54, (t(207)=-1.39, p=0.17).", "However, the slope dikerence between male and female group did not significant (z = -1.71, p =0.088), suggesting the need for larger samples to further investigate potential gender-specific ekects. associated with age after controlling for gender and logged smartphone screen time.", "However, memory performance was not associated with reporting discrepancy after controlling age and logged screen time (b=-1.98, 95%CI [-11.53, 6.63], p=0.67).", "The estimated indirect ekect was not statistically significant (ab=-0.10, 95%CI [-0.33, 0.59], p=0.68)." )), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. text.text: There is growing evidence that self-reported media use poorly reflects real use, yet selfreports remain the dominant method in media research.
Furthermore, the capacity to self-regulate smartphone use intuitively depends on how accurately one perceives that use.
Here, we directly compared self-reported and objectively logged smartphone screen time in 304 participants aged 20 to 84 years.
We found that reporting bias was strongly age-dependent: older adults underestimated their use while younger adults overestimated theirs.
The age-related reporting bias was not explained by working memory performance (2-back task).
Working memory did not mediate the association between age and reporting discrepancy.
Our findings indicate that self-reported smartphone use carry little information on real use.
We highlight the importance of objective measures of smartphone use and the need for understanding mechanisms which distort perceived use.
Imagine, when you are asked how many hours you spent on your smartphone last week, what do you usually say?
Although it sounds like a simple question, answering it is not a simple readout of a stored quantity (Dang, King, and Inzlicht 2020).
text.formatted: Although it sounds like a simple question, answering it is not a simple readout of a stored quantity <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Dang, King, and Inzlicht 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Instead, it requires complex cognitive processes to reconstruct past behavior (Knäuper et al. 2016).
text.formatted: Instead, it requires complex cognitive processes to reconstruct past behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Knäuper et al. 2016)</ref>.

text.text: You probably retrieve smartphone-relevant episodes, estimate their durations, evaluate how representative those episodes were, and integrate them into a single value.

Such reconstruction inevitably introduces discrepancies between self-reported and real behavior, a phenomenon documented across a wide range of behaviors including for smartphone use (Gorzelitz et al. 2018; Jackson et al. 2018; Parry et al. 2021; Prince et al. 2020).
text.formatted: Such reconstruction inevitably introduces discrepancies between self-reported and real behavior, a phenomenon documented across a wide range of behaviors including for smartphone use <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Gorzelitz et al. 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Jackson et al. 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Parry et al. 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Prince et al. 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, aging research has largely assumed that such reporting bias is uniform across age but whether this assumption holds remains unclear given the wellknown age-related changes in cognitive processing.
Some cognitive mechanisms have been used to explain reporting biases across domains.

Studies of sleep and physical activity among older adults have found the association between cognitive function with self-reported discrepancy between self-reported and real behavior (Calderon et al. 2024; Herbolsheimer, Riepe, and Peter 2018; Soh et al. 2025).
text.formatted: Studies of sleep and physical activity among older adults have found the association between cognitive function with self-reported discrepancy between self-reported and real behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Calderon et al. 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Herbolsheimer, Riepe, and Peter 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Soh et al. 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Notably, poorer delayed memory performance is correlated with discrepancy (Soh et al. 2025).
text.formatted: Notably, poorer delayed memory performance is correlated with discrepancy <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Soh et al. 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, accumulating evidence indicates that multiple cognitive processes involved in retrospective reporting systematically change across the lifespan, and here too memory plays a dominant role (Block, Zakay, and Hancock 1998; Di Crosta et al. 2026; Korkki et al. 2020; Vanneste et al. 2016).
text.formatted: Moreover, accumulating evidence indicates that multiple cognitive processes involved in retrospective reporting systematically change across the lifespan, and here too memory plays a dominant role <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Block, Zakay, and Hancock 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Di Crosta et al. 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Korkki et al. 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Vanneste et al. 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Taken together, those findings raise the possibility that aging may systematically influence reporting bias via changes in memory capacity.

This possibility has important implications: some reported age dikerences in behavior may reflect dikerences in the ability to retrospectively selfreported behavior rather than dikerences in the behavior itself.
Obtaining an objective measure of actual behavior is itself challenging.

Many behaviors such as sleep and physical activity, are typically captured by wearable sensors and then inferred through algorithms, introducing potential sources of measurement error between the real behavior and its recorded estimate (Evenson, Goto, and Furberg 2015; Giurgiu et al. 2025).
text.formatted: Many behaviors such as sleep and physical activity, are typically captured by wearable sensors and then inferred through algorithms, introducing potential sources of measurement error between the real behavior and its recorded estimate <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Evenson, Goto, and Furberg 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Giurgiu et al. 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Smartphone behavior okers an alternative: smartphone behaviors are captured as timestamped behavioral events, requiring relatively little transformation before they can be compared with self-report.
This provides an unusually direct opportunity to compare what people report doing with what they did.
Here, we directly examined whether the discrepancy of self-reported smartphone use is age dependent.
We quantified the discrepancy between reported and logged use, examined whether this discrepancy systematically varies as a function of age by liner regression models.
Given that memory as a key cognitive processing involved in retrospective reporting, we also explored whether memory mediated the relationship between reporting discrepancy and age.
This study draws on an existing longitudinal project designed to examine smartphone behavior and brain function across the adult lifespan in the Netherlands (Ceolini et al. 2022).
text.formatted: This study draws on an existing longitudinal project designed to examine smartphone behavior and brain function across the adult lifespan in the Netherlands <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Ceolini et al. 2022)</ref>.

text.text: From this cohort 401 participants (210 females, 91 females, 100 participants with unreported or other gender identities) who owned a personal Android smartphone and reported no history of psychiatric or neurological disorder, had the app installed at least 7 days prior to the self-reports and participated in the self-reported smartphone use segment of the study.
Ninety-seven participants were excluded due to missing smartphone data or being younger than 16 years, yielding a final sample of 304.
All participants provided written informed consent, and the project was approved by the Psychology Research Ethics Committee at Leiden University (2023-12-18-A. Ghosh-V2-5092).
Self-reported smartphone screen time.
At the beginning of the study, participants completed a series of online questionnaires including assessing smartphone use.
Among these questions, participants were asked, "How long did you use your smartphone on average per day last week?".
Participants answered it with the number of hours and minutes separately.

Participant installed an app, Tap Counter (QuantActions AG, Zurich, Switzerland), to automatically record timestamps of all screen-on and screen-ok events, as well as all smartphone touchscreen touches at the background (Balerna and Ghosh 2018).

text.text: For each participant, we extracted the smartphone logs from the seven days before the completion of the self-reported smartphone screen time.
To calculate the logged smartphone screen time, we summed up the durations of each screen-on and screen-ok event.
Sessions without any touchscreen touches were excluded as these could indicate phone generated notifications.
Then, we obtained the median value for the past week as the logged smartphone screen time.

Two-back task was used to assess participants' memory function.
Participants (n=270) completed this task via the agestudy.nl platform.
A sequence of letters was presented, and participant were asked to respond as soon as possible whenever the current letter was the same shown two trials back.
Each letter was displayed for 760 ms, with an interstimuli intervals of 2 s.
The main task consisted of three blocks and each block contains 30 trials.
Before that, participant watched a video tutorial and completed a practice session.
Memory performance was quantified using signal detection sensitivity by calculating the distance between hit rate and false alarm rate in standard deviation units.
All statistical analysis were performed in MATLAB.

To examine the convergence of selfreported and logged smartphone screen time, we fitted a liner regression analysis with self-reported screen time as the dependent variable and logged smartphone screen time as the independent variable.
The analysis was performed using fitlm.m function in MATLAB, with robust regression using the default 'bisquare' weighting function.
This model was used to estimate the reporting discrepancy for next analysis as well.
To examine the relationship between reporting discrepancy and age, multiple regression model was conducted.
Firstly, the test the model with reporting discrepancy as the dependent variables while age as independent variable.
Next, we included gender and logged screen time as a covariate into this model.
These analyses were performed using the same robust regression procedure described above.

Finally, to explore whether memory function as mediation between reporting discrepancy and age, we conducted a path model in which age predicted memory performance (a), and both age (c') and memory performance (b) predicted reporting discrepancy.
The logged screen time and gender were included as covariates in both models.
The indirect ekect was evaluated using percentile bootstrap confidence intervals based on 10,000 resamples.
Analyses were conducted in R using the lavaan package (Rosseel, 2012).

Smartphone behavior provides a valuable opportunity to address the factors underlying self-reports as objectively logged smartphone use can be directly compared with retrospective reports of the same behavior.
Our findings confirm that self-reported smartphone use does not reflect actual behavior and highlights a putative role of aging in these self-reports.
Older adults tended to underestimate their screen time, whereas younger adults tended to overestimate it.

These findings highlight the need for caution when interpreting self-reported media consumption, as apparent dikerences in behavior may partly reflect age-related dikerences in reporting rather than dikerences in the behavior itself.
We found that discrepancies between self-reported and objectively logged screen time were pervasive consistent with previous findings (Horwood, Anglim, and Mallawaarachchi 2021; Tkaczyk et al. 2024).

text.text: Why do such discrepancies arise?
We observed substantial variability in reporting discrepancies across participants.
One possibility is that the characteristics of smartphone behavior influence the smartphone self-reports.

Individuals diker substantially in how they use their smartphones, including the apps they use, screen time, multi-days use rhythms, and the temporal structure of their behavior (Ceolini and Ghosh 2023; Ceolini, Ridderinkhof, and Ghosh 2024; Pfister and Ghosh 2020; Sekara et al. 2021; Wan, Ridderinkhof, and Ghosh 2026).
text.formatted: Individuals diker substantially in how they use their smartphones, including the apps they use, screen time, multi-days use rhythms, and the temporal structure of their behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Ceolini and Ghosh 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Ceolini, Ridderinkhof, and Ghosh 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Pfister and Ghosh 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Sekara et al. 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Wan, Ridderinkhof, and Ghosh 2026)</ref>.

text.text: However, reporting discrepancies were not significantly associated with objectively logged screen time, suggesting that individual dikerences in overall smartphone use cannot simply account for the observed variability in reporting.
Alternatively, cognitive process underlying self-reports may vary from person to person, and the reporting discrepancies did systematically vary with age.
Older adults tended to underestimate their screen time, whereas younger adults tended to overestimate it.
However, we were not able to attribute this to a specific process as memory performance did not mediate the association between age and reporting discrepancy in the present study.

Although age-related changes in memory have been extensively documented, evidence from real-world contexts suggests that age-related dikerences in episodic memory may not always translate directly into dikerences in everyday memory performance (Folville et al. 2020).
text.formatted: Although age-related changes in memory have been extensively documented, evidence from real-world contexts suggests that age-related dikerences in episodic memory may not always translate directly into dikerences in everyday memory performance <ref type="bibr">(Folville et al. 2020)</ref>.

text.text: The relationship between smartphone use and cognitive function may therefore be more complex (Hartanto et al. 2023; Liebherr et al. 2020).

text.text: Alternatively, age-related dikerences in beliefs and expectations about smartphone use may influence retrospective reports.
Younger adults may be more likely to perceive themselves as being "constantly" on their smartphones, whereas older adults may view their smartphone use as relatively limited.
Such stereotypes could bias retrospective estimates independently of actual behavior.

It is also possible that older and younger adults diker in what they consider to constitute "smartphone use" potentially leading them to base their estimates on dikerent aspects of their interactions with the device (K. Kaye et al. 2020).

text.text: These possibilities remain speculative and warrant further investigation.
Our findings have important implications for both media use and behavioral aging research.
Apparent age dikerences based on self-reported measures cannot automatically be interpreted as dikerences in actual behavior; they may partly reflect systematic age-related dikerences in reporting.
These findings highlight the need for caution when interpreting self-reported measures in behavioral aging research.
Whenever feasible, objective measures should be used to characterize age-related changes in everyday behavior (Sekara et al. 2021).
